cue: Hold still, as a spider holds its web. Only what moves reaches you.
rows: A Golden Silk Spider feels its prey through the silk, and a trapped insect shakes the web 5 to 30 times a second. The shaking arrives ten to thirty times stronger on some legs than on others, which gives the direction.
Most spiders have eight eyes and few see well. Most register little more than changes between light and dark, and spiders that build webs lean on the shaking of the silk.
A wandering spider resolves nothing finer than about 2 degrees, under a hundredth of your sharpness. The picture borrows that figure for web builders.
A wandering spider stops following flicker between 4.3 and 8.6 times a second, a seventh of your rate or less, so movement smears into trails.

Where the phone’s motion sensors or its microphone are switched on, a knock on the phone or on the table it lies on, or a low sound, sends ripples across the picture. They stand in for a shaking web, and the ripples are the app’s own drawing.
A bridge spider turns toward a loudspeaker three metres away, because its web moves with the air and works as a listening surface up to 10,000 times larger than its body.
Wolf spiders have four large rear eyes backed by a mirror layer, which shines back in a flashlight beam and helps them spot movement in dim light. This picture leaves that out.

With &draw=web the picture carries a drawn web that shakes and flashes with knocks and sounds. With &draw=air, breath on the microphone ruffles the picture. With &draw=buzz the phone buzzes at a knock. Each drawing is the app's.

rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: Most spiders have eight eyes, and only a few families, Dysderidae, Sicariidae and Oonopidae, have six, so you very likely have eight. The secondary eyes of spiders are regarded as motion detectors, and you very likely have some of these. Nobody has measured how your eyes are built or what each of them does for you.
rows.note: Left out R1-R5 and R8 (single species or genus findings); R5 only applies to the Giant Lichen Orbweaver.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see. The few spiders that have been measured differ widely: the big front eyes of a Portia jumping spider read about 12 cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30, while the large rear middle eyes of the net-casting spider Dinopis read about a third of a cycle a degree. Neither figure can be carried over to you.
rows.note: No record covers any listed species or its genus, so no figure is carried; the row names only the measured spiders.

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see. In one crab spider, Xysticus cristatus, the front middle eyes stop seeing flicker at about 10 flashes a second, where a human stops at about 60. That figure belongs to that crab spider's eyes alone, and no one has measured it in your species.
rows.note: Left out R2 (Cupiennius salei): its quote does not clearly state a flicker limit.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: Some spider eyes have a tapetum, a reflective layer behind the light-sensing cells, but in spiders it is always missing from the front middle pair. In two Argiope species the light-sensing cells of the eyes become more sensitive at night, and in the nocturnal Araneus ventricosus a front middle eye also follows a daily rhythm of sensitivity. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see, or whether your other eyes have a tapetum.
rows.note: Left out the huntsman and lynx spider tapetum records and the Deinopis starlight record because the row is about most species; say if you want per-species rows.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: In the big front eyes of the jumping spider Plexippus, cells sense ultraviolet and green only, and another jumping spider, Evarcha, picked orange or blue stripes over plain surfaces of every shade of gray it was offered. In two garden spiders, Argiope bruennichi and Argiope amoena, the front eyes have three kinds of color-sensing cell, for ultraviolet, blue and green. Nobody has measured which kinds of color-sensing cell you have, or whether you can tell colors apart.
rows.note: Left out the count of gray shades and the wavelength figures, since neither has a job in the row.

rows.title: The web
rows.text: If you are a golden silk spider, the insects caught in your web shake it 5 to 30 times a second, while air stirred by a flying insect seldom makes you attack and often makes you lift your forelegs. If you are a six-spotted fishing spider, you jump away from a striking frog, and the fine hairs called trichobothria that sense moving air are necessary and sufficient for that jump. For most other spiders, nobody has measured how you sense vibration or moving air.
rows.note: Left out the orb weaver and web builder statements (R12-R14) because they are grade g and this row is graded i.
